t.3.60.1: Bṛhadaśva said: When Nala had gone away, O king, Damayantī of the lovely hips, her weariness gone, awoke, frightened, in the desolate forest.
t.3.60.2: Not seeing her husband, she, filled with grief and sorrow and terrified, cried out loudly to the Naiṣadha, "O great king!"
t.3.60.3: Alas, my protector! Alas, great king! Alas, my lord, why do you abandon me? Alas, I am slain, I am undone, I am afraid in this desolate forest!
t.3.60.4: Surely, great king, you know dharma and speak the truth; how then, having spoken such a falsehood, have you gone away, abandoning me while I slept?
t.3.60.5: How will you go away, abandoning your obedient and devoted wife, especially when she has done you no wrong and the wrong was done to you by another?
t.3.60.7: Enough of this jest, so much of it, O bull among men! I am frightened, O invincible one; show yourself, my lord.
t.3.60.6: O lord of men, will you be able to make true toward me those words which you spoke long ago in the presence of the guardians of the world?
t.3.60.8: You are seen, you are seen, O king! Here you stand, O Naiṣadha, having hidden yourself behind the bushes; why do you not answer me?
t.3.60.9: Alas, lord of kings, it is cruel that you do not embrace and comfort me as I lament here, fallen into such a state, O king!
t.3.60.10: I do not grieve for myself, nor for anything else at all; it is for you I grieve, O king, wondering how you will fare all alone.
t.3.60.11: How, O king, will you fare, thirsty, hungry and worn out with weariness, at evening beneath the roots of trees, when you do not see me?
t.3.60.12: Then she, afflicted with fierce grief and as if blazing with anguish, ran about this way and that, weeping in her distress.
t.3.60.13: Again and again the young woman springs up, again and again she falls down, overwhelmed; again and again she cowers in fear, again and again she cries out and weeps.
t.3.60.14: Tormented by fierce grief, sighing again and again and overwhelmed, Bhaimī, the woman devoted to her husband, came out and, weeping, spoke.
t.3.60.15: May that being through whose curse the Naiṣadha, stricken with grief, suffers sorrow come to know a sorrow even greater than that sorrow.
t.3.60.16: The wicked one who has thus wronged Nala, whose mind is free of sin, may he, having met with sorrow greater than this, live a joyless life.
t.3.60.17: Lamenting thus, she, the wife of the great-souled king, went searching for her husband in the forest frequented by beasts of prey.
t.3.60.18: Then, like one gone mad, Bhīma's daughter, lamenting here and there, ran this way and that, crying again and again, "Alas, alas, O king!"
t.3.60.19: Her, wasting away exceedingly, crying out like an osprey hen, grieving much and piteously, lamenting again and again.
t.3.60.21: Being seized by the crocodile and overcome by grief, she did not grieve for herself so much as she grieved for the Naiṣadha.
t.3.60.20: As Bhaimī, who had suddenly come upon it, wandered close by, a huge-bodied python, a seizing beast gripped by hunger, seized her.
t.3.60.22: Alas, my lord, why do you not rush to me here in the forest, as I am being swallowed in this wilderness by this serpent, as though I had no protector?
t.3.60.23: How will you fare, O Naiṣadha, when, freed from evil and having regained your understanding, your mind and your wealth, you remember me once more?
t.3.60.24: O Naiṣadha, tiger among kings, giver of honor, when you are weary, tormented by hunger and utterly exhausted, who will dispel your fatigue?
t.3.60.25: A hunter of deer, roaming by chance through the dense forest, heard her crying out and rushed swiftly toward her.
t.3.60.26: Seeing her, the wide-eyed one, thus seized by the serpent, the hunter, hurrying, rushed swiftly toward her.
t.3.60.28: The hunter freed her and washed her with water, and when he had comforted her and she had taken food, he then questioned her, O Bhārata.
t.3.60.27: With a sharpened blade the hunter struck at the serpent's mouth and, cutting it open, brought that snake down, leaving it motionless.
t.3.60.29: Whose are you, O fawn-eyed one, and how have you come to the forest? And how, O beautiful lady, have you fallen into this great distress?
t.3.60.30: Being thus questioned by him, O lord of the people, Damayantī told him all this just as it had happened, O Bhārata.
t.3.60.31: Her, clad in half a garment, with full hips and breasts, of delicate and flawless limbs, her face like the full moon,
t.3.60.32: Seeing her, with eyes fringed by curving lashes and so sweet of speech, the deer-hunter fell under the sway of desire.
t.3.60.33: Then the hunter, tormented by desire, tried to soothe her with smooth words prefaced by gentleness, and the beautiful woman understood that.
t.3.60.34: But Damayantī, devoted to her husband, perceiving that he was wicked, was seized by fierce rage and seemed to blaze up with fury.
t.3.60.35: But that base, evil-minded man, burning with desire to violate her, judged her to be unassailable, like a blazing tongue of fire.
t.3.60.36: But Damayantī, stricken with sorrow and bereft of her husband and her kingdom, in that time of suffering beyond the reach of words, cursed him in her wrath, so it is said.
t.3.60.37: As surely as I do not think of anyone other than the Naiṣadha even in my mind, so surely may this vile hunter, who lives by killing beasts, fall down lifeless.
t.3.60.38: But the moment those words had been spoken by her, that hunter fell lifeless upon the earth, like a tree consumed by fire.
